But despite this, however, AdS/CFT may be pointing towards something deeper.
It suggests that gravity and space-time might not be fundamental, but emergent, woven from more basic quantum interactions on a lower dimensional boundary.
And so, even though our universe didn't appear to be built from anti-de Sitter space, Maldacena's duality hinted at a broader principle, that the fabric of space itself could be a kind of hologram.

And nowhere is this holographic principle more sharply tested than with black holes, the most extreme objects in the universe, where general relativity and quantum mechanics directly contradict each other.
And resolving that contradiction is precisely what string theory was built to do.
In particular, black holes raise a question that neither theory can answer alone.
What happens to information that falls in?
This is the infamous black hole information paradox.
And to explain this, the court now calls Jacob Bekenstein to the stand.
Born in Mexico City in 1947, Bekenstein saw the spiritual side of science.
"I look at the world as a product of God.
He set very specific laws, and we delight in discovering them through scientific work, he once told the Israeli newspaper Haaretz.
But if there's any place in the universe that stands as the antithesis of heaven, it's probably a black hole.
Inescapable chasms in the very fabric of space-time, they relentlessly heave and hoard.
Matter is drawn inexorably inwards towards an event horizon, torn limb from limb before vanishing over the edge of the gravitational waterfall, gone forever.
From 1972, Bekenstein founded the field of black hole thermodynamics, an achievement that would eerily foreshadow Maldacena's work a quarter of a century later.
For at its heart, thermodynamics is the study of a property known as entropy, a measure of how many ways a system can be rearranged internally without changing its outward appearance.
More possibilities means higher entropy.
And so, to understand this, imagine hurling a book over the event horizon of a black hole.
According to general relativity, black holes can be completely described by just three properties: their mass, their charge, and their spin.
Of course, your book adds a tiny bit of mass, but all the fine-grained details about what was on each page, the carefully crafted characters and narrative arcs, appear to vanish.
And therein lies a problem, for the second law of thermodynamics explicitly forbids the destruction of entropy.
It must always increase or remain constant.
Bekenstein's breakthrough was to propose that the black hole responds to your book by increasing the area of its event horizon and that this area functions as a kind of entropy.
And in doing so, he preserved the second law and hinted at a deeper truth.
That the black hole's boundary somehow stores information about everything inside.
That sounds a lot like AdS/CFT correspondence.
But a deeper problem remained.
In 1974, Stephen Hawking showed that black holes aren't entirely black.
Indeed, over immense time scales, it was revealed that the black hole can evaporate completely.
This therefore created a new paradox.
Hawking radiation was featureless, carrying no imprint of what fell in.
When the black hole was gone for good, so was all the information it once contained.
This violated not just thermodynamics, but the core of quantum mechanics, which insists that information cannot be destroyed.
And this was the paradox.
A conflict not between specific theories, but between the foundational rules of physics themselves.
And it would take the machinery of string theory and the radical duality of AdS/CFT to begin to resolve it.
And here, perhaps, the courtroom reaches its tensest moment.
What began as a case about strings and particles has become a trial over the very nature of space, time, and information itself.
Let's return once more to our grand AdS/CFT library.
From inside the library, when a black hole forms and eventually evaporates, it seems as though information about what it swallowed has been lost.
A book thrown into the gravitational abyss appears to vanish without a trace, but the screen on the boundary wall, the boundary quantum theory, keeps a perfect record.
In the language of the screen, nothing is ever truly lost.
The ADS/CFT correspondence tells us that these two descriptions, the interior view with gravity and the screen's quantum field theory without gravity, are mathematically equivalent.
So, if the screen evolves in a way that preserves information, then the entire library must, as well.
What looked like destruction from a gravitational perspective is, from the boundary's point of view, just a particularly complicated translation.
And so, the black hole information paradox becomes not a failure of physics, but a sign that space, gravity, and information are woven together more tightly than we'd ever imagined.
But, of course, though ADS/CFT may seem to provide a compelling resolution to the black hole information paradox, it does so in a universe we don't inhabit.
After all, we don't live in anti-de Sitter space.
And so, again, the theory's insights are deep and possibly universal, but we still don't know how to apply it to the real universe.
And so, with Maldacena's duality, the courtroom reeled.
Beauty had taken the stand in its purest form.
An entire universe projected onto a two-dimensional screen.
For the defense, it was a masterstroke.
For the prosecution, just more speculation in silk robes, the emperor's new clothes.
Once more, the jury was suspended between wonder and doubt, dazzled by beauty, but starved of proof.
Indeed, there were those that loathed this approach to physics, not least the fact that the theory is currently impossible to test or falsify.

Some argued that physicists were so desperate to reconcile quantum theory with gravity that they lost sight of the most fundamental aspect of a good scientific theory, that it should make testable predictions.
Physicist Lee Smolin once remarked, "It's not really a theory.
It's a conjecture about a theory that we would love to believe in." The prosecution pounced.
To them, Maldacena's entire testimony reeked of speculation.
No crime scene, no fingerprints, no verifiable timeline, just elegant conjectures stacked atop untestable assumptions.
Impressively told circumstantial evidence, at best.
Theoretical physics, they reminded the jury, should not be judged by aesthetic appeal, but by experimental accountability.
Until AdS/CFT made contact with measurable reality, until it predicted something nature could confirm or deny, it remained, in the prosecution's eyes, an exquisite, outlandish guess.
Not for the first time, the defense team was scrambling.
Then, just as they began to regroup, the universe threw them another potentially catastrophic curveball.
You may find that your most elegant theory, the one you like the best, is simply wrong.
It is the opening days of 1998.
Bill Clinton is president.
Elton John's re-worked Candle in the Wind, a tribute to Princess Diana, is finishing its 14-week run at the top of the US charts.
Titanic is still packing cinemas.
And against this cultural backdrop, the American Astronomical Society is holding its annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
Journalists and scientists packed the room to hear from astronomer Saul Perlmutter.
On the screen, a decades worth of data reduced to dots and lines.
What he is about to reveal would later win him a share of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Yet in the courtroom of theoretical physics, this was a hostile witness, one summoned from a completely different field with no loyalty to string theory.
And the evidence Perlmutter presented would leave the defense scrambling and hand the prosecution an explosive new line of attack.
The vast majority of astronomers and cosmologists accept that the universe began in an event known as the Big Bang nearly 14 billion years ago.
It started out unimaginably small, far tinier than an atom, and has been expanding ever since, ballooning into the cosmos we see today.
But by now, many eons later, that expansion should be slowing down.
The gravitational pull of all the stuff in the universe, stars, gas, galaxies, dark matter, ought to be applying the brakes.
And in the mid-1990s, as the second superstring revolution roiled through theoretical physics, two teams of astronomers had been busy trying to confirm that deceleration.
It was supposed to just be a routine check.
But when Perlmutter announced his team's results at that press conference in early 1998, they stunned the astronomical community.
For string theorists, it was a bombshell in open court, a line of evidence they hadn't anticipated, and one they had no ready answer for.
Both teams have been using exploding stars called type 1A supernovae to track the expansion history of the universe.
These cosmic detonations occur in binary systems where a dead, dense white dwarf orbits alongside an ordinary star.
Over time, the white dwarf's gravity siphons material from its companion, slowly growing heavier.
But its appetite has a hard limit.
Once the white dwarf nears a critical mass, about 1.4 times that of the sun, known as the Chandrasekhar limit, it becomes unstable.
A wave of thermonuclear reactions rips through it and the star is blown apart.
But what makes type 1A supernovae so useful is that they all explode with roughly the same amount of fuel.
That means they all shine with roughly the same intrinsic brightness.
Astronomers call them standard candles and by comparing how bright they appear to how bright they should be, they can determine their distance.
The dimmest are the furthest away.
Except the two rival teams, Perlmutter's Supernova Cosmology Project and the High-Z Supernova Search Team, both found something deeply unexpected.
The distant supernovae were too dim.
Not just farther than expected, but as if space had expanded more than it should have since their light began its journey towards us.
And the only explanation was shocking.
The expansion of the universe wasn't slowing down.
It was speeding up.
Even today, astronomers have no definitive answer as to why this is happening.
The accelerating expansion is usually put down to something called dark energy, a shadowy entity whose potency only grows as the universe ages.
What dark energy actually is, however, remains, well, dark.
But what we do know is that dark energy implies something about a term in Einstein's equations, the cosmological constant, usually denoted by the Greek letter lambda.
Einstein originally introduced it as a mathematical fix to hold the universe still.
And when Edwin Hubble discovered the universe was actually expanding, Einstein realized his error.
But lambda wasn't a mistake after all.
Today, it's clear that the cosmological constant, the amount of energy that occupies all of empty space, or something acting like that, is real, and it's driving the acceleration.
And more than just setting space's expansion rate, lambda also affects its geometry.
If this energy is negative, the universe has negative curvature.
And if it's positive, as the supernova data seem to suggest, the universe has positive curvature.
And this was and is a big problem for string theory.
We've seen a negative curvature before.
When Polchinski stacked D3 branes in our holographic library, the mass and charge of the branes warped the space, curving the library walls inwards.
Indeed, that's anti-de Sitter, ADS, geometry with negative curvature.
But now, a fundamental cosmological measurement was telling us that the real universe curves the other way.
The walls don't cave in.
In geometric terms, we didn't live in an anti-de Sitter space with negative curvature, but in a de Sitter-like universe, where the curvature is positive, and the expansion accelerates indefinitely.
And that's not merely a mismatch, it strikes at the heart of the most mathematically mature part of M-theory.
AdS/CFT, for all its evidence, turned out to be built on a geometry that clearly clashes with astronomical observations.
Speaking in 2001, Ed Witten said, "I don't know of any clear way to get to sitter space from string theory or M-theory." This was a damning admission from string theory's biggest star witness.
The defense was once again on the ropes.
With no explanation for dark energy, the prosecution smelt blood.
And though what followed wasn't a knockout blow, it might be the defense's last chance to stay on its feet.
Desperate, the defense team called Renata Kallosh to the stand.
Kallosh was born in 1943 in the culturally rich city of Chernivtsi, now part of Ukraine, amid the upheaval of World War II.
She came of age during the Khrushchev thaw, a period of relative openness and reform following Stalin's death.
Against this backdrop, Kallosh moved to Moscow to study physics.
And by 1968, she'd earned her PhD from the capital's prestigious Lebedev Physical Institute.
She would also find love there.
Seminars on cosmological phase transitions are typically known as hotbeds of romance, but it was during one such seminar that she caught the eye of fellow physicist Andrei Linde.
They began talking about physics, and 2 years later they met again, this time at Lake Ladoga near St.
"When I was leaving Ladoga, I kept Renata's hand in mine just a second longer than I was supposed to," Linde recalls.
"A few months later, we were married." The couple recently celebrated their golden wedding anniversary.
Kallosh and Linde quickly became a physics power couple.

As the Soviet Union began to collapse, they left together, first for CERN, and then in 1990 to accept joint professorships at Stanford University, home to one of the world's leading centers for cosmology and theoretical physics.
And they were still at Stanford in 2003 when they helped develop an idea that might rescue string theory from the existential quagmire brought on by the discovery of dark energy.
Working alongside Shamit Kachru and Sandip Trivedi, they devised what became known as the KKLT mechanism, a moniker formed from the initials of their surnames.
Back in the 1980s, amid the first superstring revolution, physicists had made headway in curling up the extra dimensions of string theory.
The work of Calabi and Yau offered a way to fold the origami of the universe into intricate, compact shapes known as Calabi-Yau manifolds.
But even by the early 21st century, this approach faced a serious problem.
The folds weren't stable.
The size and shape of these extra dimensions could fluctuate wildly, leading to universes that were either unstable or unrecognizable.
And so, like the Green-Schwarz mechanism before it, the KKLT mechanism was a patch, a fix for a deeper flaw.
First, it introduced fluxes, fields that thread through the folds of the extra dimensions, acting like invisible tape to hold the shape in place and prevent it from warping.
But that alone wasn't enough.
These solutions still tended to produce universes with negative curvature, anti-de Sitter space.
And so, to fix this, KKLT introduced anti-branes, objects with the opposite energy and charge to regular D-branes.
Adding them tips the balance, finally producing a universe with positive curvature, just like the de Sitter space implied by the supernova results.
But, it turned out that there were a lot of ways to add fluxes and anti-branes to Calabi-Yau manifolds.
Each one produces a different version of string theory, resulting in a different version of the universe with its own laws of physics, particles, and forces.
And this vast expanse of possibilities is known as the string theory landscape.
But this landscape doesn't contain just a handful of different string theories, or even a thousand, not even a million, billion, or trillion different ways, but at least 100 quindecillion.
That's a one followed by 500 zeros.
It's hard to do justice to just how big a number that is.
Compared to these 10 to 500 possible universes, the number of galaxies, stars, or even seconds since the Big Bang are mere rounding errors.
Jacob Bekenstein once calculated the limit of how much information can be stored in a given region of space.
And so if the entire observable universe were a cosmic hard drive, it could hold around 10 to the power of 122 bits of information.
So adding the KKLT mechanism suddenly gave us possible versions of string theory than there is information available in the entire universe to list them.
No matter how smart we are, no matter the size of the computers we build, we can't ever hope to catalog, simulate, or analyze them all, even in principle.
The computational and physical limits of the universe make that utterly impossible.
And so if string theory had been accused of untestability before, it was now, in the eyes of its critics, irreparably so.
To the prosecution, the defense had exchanged uniqueness for a wilderness of alibis.
One such critic, Lee Smolin, didn't mince his words.
If an attempt to construct a unique theory of nature leads to 10 to the power of 500 theories, that approach has been reduced to absurdity.
The defense argued that this is simply what frontier physics looks like, messy, abstract, and occasionally lost in its own beauty.
The prosecution, however, saw something very different, a theory not grounded in evidence, but permanently insulated from it.
And so, if string theory's defense team were to stop the judge and jury throwing out the case for good, they had some key blanks to fill in.
If the universe is accelerating, not just coasting, but racing away from itself, then we're dealing with something far stranger than anyone had planned for.
Instead of a small tweak to the cosmic script, it was a complete rewrite of the opening scene.
The trial was no longer just about strings or particles.

With so many possibilities now on the table, the courtroom had become something else entirely, a grand inquest into not just how the universe exists, but why this particular version of it emerged from the vastness of possibility.
And whatever the answer was, it wouldn't be local.
It wouldn't be small, and it certainly wouldn't leave the early universe untouched.
The great tragedy of science, the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact.
The sun rises slowly over a picture of serenity, a glassy pond with not a ripple to be seen.
A cool early morning mist clings to the calm waters as dragonflies dance between the reeds, the silence only broken by the occasional chirp of a cricket or croak of a frog.
Though it may not seem like it, this picturesque pond shares a lot in common with the modern universe.
It's seemingly calm, balanced, and most importantly, self-contained.
Indeed, according to the theory of the Big Bang, this cosmic pond grew from a tiny puddle about 14 billion years ago.
But like any seemingly still pond, you'd expect to find disturbances beneath the surface, eddies, whirlpools, and currents.
Yet instead of this, the more physicists studied the universe, the more unsettlingly still it became.
The deeper they looked, the more uncanny the calm.
And so in a sense, it wasn't what they saw that was alarming.
It was what they didn't see.
To begin with, there was the flatness problem.
Just like the surface of the serene pond, space today appears to be very close to what astronomers call flat.
In other words, it has almost no curvature at all.
Any tiny deviation from flatness early on should have become exaggerated as space expanded, warping the surface into something visibly bent today.
And yet instead, it's astonishingly smooth.
At first glance, there are two possible explanations for this.
Perhaps space was perfectly flat to begin with, and so simply stayed that way as it grew.
A serene puddle growing into a serene pond.
But the odds of that happening by chance are astronomically low.
The second option is that the pond ballooned so enormously that any initial ripples were ironed out, flattened by sheer size.
But the standard Big Bang model doesn't allow for nearly enough expansion to do the job.
And then, there's the horizon problem.
Even though the pond is now vast, too wide for a ripple to have crossed from one bank to the other since it formed, the entire surface looks perfectly coordinated.
No currents, no temperature differences, every part of the pond seems to have agreed on the same conditions.
And that shouldn't be possible.
For one side of a system to know about the other, to equalize, synchronize, or share information, something has to travel between them.
A ripple, a current, a message in a bottle, something.
But in our expanding pond, there simply hasn't been time for that.
The banks are too far apart.
There hasn't been enough time for ripples or information to reach from one side to the other, for everything to even out.
The speed of light simply isn't fast enough to cover the distance in the time the universe has existed, and yet its opposite sides still appear identical.
And finally, there's the monopole problem.
Predicted particles that, like mythical leviathans lurking in the deep, should be swimming through the cosmos in droves.
Magnetic poles without a partner, a south without a north, a north without a south.
Theories that try to unify the three non-gravitational forces suggest that at high energies, the early universe should have produced huge numbers of them.
And yet, we've never seen one.
That's a serious problem for any theory aiming to describe physics at the highest energies, string theory included.
And so, each of these three problems alone was troubling.
The three of them together was damning.
The Big Bang was our best model of the early universe, but it was leaking at the seams.
If no solution could be found, it might have to be abandoned altogether.
And if even the Big Bang couldn't be trusted, how could grander frameworks like superstring theory, which sought to unify all of physics, hope to succeed?
Luckily for superstring and the Big Bang theory, one man had a single idea that could patch every leak at once.
The court to call is Alan Guth to the stand.
Born in 1947 in New Brunswick, New Jersey, Guth skipped his senior year of high school and enrolled at MIT at just 17, earning a bachelor's, master's, and a PhD all in quick succession.
He began his career in particle physics studying quarks before shifting his focus to cosmology in the mid-1970s, drawn by puzzles like magnetic monopoles and the flatness of space.
Yet Guth struggled and went from temporary post to temporary post until late one night in December 1979, he experienced what he described at the time as a spectacular realization.
Guth figured out the period of rapid exponential expansion could solve not one, but all three Big Bang problems.
And by 1981, he had formally proposed what we now know as cosmic inflation, and his career, understandably, took off.
Inflation is like an underground pipe beneath the pond.
It provides a sort of pressure surge that for the briefest moment blasts huge quantities of water in from below.
The puddle doesn't just grow, it erupts.
Then, the pipe shuts off, leaving the pond to expand at a slower, steadier pace.

According to the theory, this initial inflationary phase saw the universe's size skyrocket from considerably smaller than an atom to about the size of a grapefruit in just a trillionth of a trillionth of a trillionth of a second, doubling in size roughly 80 times.
That may not sound like much, but by the end of inflation, the universe was roughly 10 to the power of 78 times bigger than it had been at the start.
To put that number into context, imagine taking an ordinary shipping container and then expanding it by the same amount.
Suddenly, it would be larger than the entire observable universe.
But how did this relatively straightforward addition solve all the problems of the Big Bang?
Well, the flatness problem hinged on the fact that there hadn't been enough expansion since the Big Bang to smooth out any initial wrinkles.
But inflation adds in the extra required expansion.
Similarly, the horizon problem argued that there hasn't been enough time for ripples to travel between every part of the pond.
Add in the extra expansion from inflation, and suddenly the puddle can start much smaller, much more interconnected, and still be capable of becoming the enormous pond we see today.
And finally, what about the missing monopoles?
Well, inflation solves that, too.

If monopoles were formed in the early universe, they would have been diluted by inflation's vast expansion of space, stretched so thinly across the cosmic pond that we'd expect to find hardly any at all.
At first, inflation looked like a miracle cure.
It fixed the flatness and horizon problems, and even swept the monopoles under the cosmic rug.
The Guth's original idea, although highly elegant in theory, didn't quite work in practice.
His version of inflation ended too violently, leaving behind a universe riddled with bubbles.
And so, as it happened many times before in physics, Guth's original model was beautiful, but when pressed, it cracked under cross-examination.
The defense would need a smoother, more controlled version of the same idea.
And that refinement would one day dramatically intersect with the world of string theory, and it came from a familiar face, Andrei Linde.
Guth's inflation research was too abrupt, like the underground pipe had burst.
Linde added the equivalent of a pressure valve.
The water still rushed in, expanding the pond dramatically, but now in a smoother, more controlled fashion.
The surface could stay calm, coherent.
And that wasn't the end of it.
For Linde's version, the valve didn't simply shut off all at once.
One region of the pond might stop swelling and begin settling, but others could keep expanding.
Some of those regions would even spawn new valves of their own, launching entirely new ponds.
And this process would never end.
Our serene pond, just one amongst countless others, each with its own currents and contours, shaped by the exact circumstances of its birth.
In other words, a vast and expansive landscape of ponds, with each one having its own particles, fundamental forces, and laws of physics.
If this idea sounds familiar, it should.
It's an eerie parallel of the string theory landscape.
And so, here was a completely separate theory, one born from an entirely different perspective, arriving at the same unsettling conclusion.
A vast multitude of universes, each with its own unique physics fingerprint.
Fixing the Big Bang theory suddenly brought it into closer alignment with superstring theory.
The defense's case began to glisten.
But, just as the two theories seem to be converging into something grander, deeper questions began to bubble up.
Could these lush ponds, so elegantly imagined, be nothing more than mirages?
To answer this question, the court summons Cumrun Vafa.
Vafa was born in 1960 in Tehran, the capital of Iran, during a period of profound political turbulence.
The Shah was in the midst of a sweeping modernization campaign known as the White Revolution.
When Vafa was four, Ayatollah Khomeini, a fierce critic of the Shah's reforms, was exiled.
That same year, the Iranian Prime Minister was assassinated in the street.
And so with all of this happening around him, the young Vafa turned his eyes a little higher, to the moon.
"Whenever I would look at the moon, it was bothering me as to why it wouldn't fall to the ground." He would later recall.

"That fact stuck with me, and also why other people were not bothered by it, and treated it as if it were irrelevant." These musings would kick-start a lifelong love affair with the biggest questions about our universe.
This ensuing quest for answers took Vafa first to MIT, then to Princeton, where he completed his PhD in 1985 under the watchful eye of Ed Witten.
And by 2008, he'd made such important contributions to string theory that he was awarded the prestigious Dirac Medal alongside Juan Maldacena and Joseph Polchinski.
And arguably Vafa's most provocative insight had come 3 years before, in 2005.
A sharp, unsettling idea that threatened to throw both string theory and inflationary cosmology into disarray.
Welcome to the swampland.
Vafa looked out across the seemingly boundless landscape of inflationary ponds, each one a possible universe with its own shape and physics, and asked a simple question.
Were any of them actually compatible with string theory?
And in case after case, the answer came back a resounding no.
No matter how you tweak the geometry or rearrange the ingredients, these pond-like universes refused to form.
Or worse, they emerged only by violating principles string theory seems to uphold everywhere else, like how forces should behave or how light particles can be.
In other words, not every mathematically consistent pond is actually physically viable.
Some of them may look placid and still, but step in and you'll find yourself sinking deep into the mud.
What had seemed like a serene pond turns out to be a slurried, stinking mess.
Together, these boggy outcrops make up Vafa's swampland.
A murky, unstable region of the inflationary landscape that cannot be derived from string theory, no matter how hard you try.
Swampland had serious teeth.
Vafa's conjectures aren't proven, but they function like legal precedent, setting the boundaries any defense must reckon with.
And so what once seemed like safe theoretical ground was suddenly treacherous.
Vafa wasn't just surveying the landscape, he was issuing injunctions.
Entire regions were now off-limits.
Vafa and others now began deriving specific mathematical tripwires, constraints that any viable universe must avoid.
Many existing theories stumbled right into them.
One of the biggest casualties was Kallosh-Linde's KKLT team mechanism.
Most known KKLT-type solutions sit squarely in Vafa's swampland.
This is a massive problem for string theorists because they need the KKLT mechanism to stabilize the theory and make it compatible with the accelerating expansion of the universe.
And indeed, Vafa's tripwires also entangle the theory of inflation itself.
In particular, they hit slow-roll inflation hard, the gentle controlled expansion described by Linde.
According to the swampland criteria, the conditions needed for such a smooth and steady growth may simply not be allowed.
The process unfolds too slowly or stretches too far or relies on a kind of delicate balance that string theory seems unwilling to permit.
For critics, this was damning.
String theory couldn't comfortably accommodate the best-known explanations for either dark energy or inflation.

If the swampland conjectures are right, then two of the most widely accepted pillars of modern cosmology are mutually incompatible with string theory, not flawed approximations, fundamentally incompatible.
Although inflation does at least have one advantage over KKLT, it might be testable.
One of the most promising tests comes in the form of primordial gravitational waves.
Inflation should have left its mark either through subtle distortions in the light leftover from the Big Bang or as faint waves still traveling through the universe today.
And several experiments are hunting for them.
Ground-based observatories like BICEP and the Simons Observatory scan the sky for signatures in the leftover light.
Soon, a space-based mission will join the chase.

LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, scheduled for launch in the 2030s, LISA will be the first gravitational wave observatory in space, exquisitely sensitive to low-frequency waves the ground-based detectors can't catch.
If LISA does see the right kind of background signal, it could offer direct evidence that inflation really did shake the universe into being.
But of course, even this wouldn't resolve the deeper question.
For proving inflation shaped our pond is one thing, but proving it filled a multiverse of ponds is quite another.
Eternal inflation may be compelling, but it remains difficult, maybe impossible, to falsify.
Indeed, critics have long warned that it risks slipping from science into metaphysics.
Paul Steinhardt, one of the original architects of inflation, has since become one of its most vocal detractors.
He now argues that inflation has become a self-justifying idea, impossible to rule out and ever more baroque in its defense.
It's the same criticism we've seen thrown at string theory time and time again.
And so, we reach an impasse.
Inflation may be right, but it's slippery.
KKLT may be beautiful, but it's inadmissible.
The case had grown enormous, a legal skyscraper of claims and counterclaims.
But at its foundation sat one quiet, unproven assumption, supersymmetry.
Indeed, the entire defense rested on it.
After all, there could be no superstring theory without supersymmetry.
And yet now, after decades, the court was finally ready to test it.
Supersymmetry is the distinctive prediction of string theory that is most likely to be discovered experimentally.
The sprawling ice sheets of Antarctica are a white, bleak wasteland.
There is nothing for miles save for snowstorms and blizzards.
Yet, as we converge on the geographic South Pole, human-made castles rise above the permafrost.
For here, on the high plateau of Antarctica, some 2,835 m above sea level, is the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station.
And among the dozens of buildings that dominate the otherwise desolate landscape is IceCube, a state-of-the-art neutrino observatory.
And yet, the truly impressive part of IceCube is found underground.
In 2005, the very same year Cumrun Vafa went public with Swampland, engineers began using drilling towers and warm water hoses to bore deep holes into the Antarctic ice.
Into each, they lowered long strings with detectors hanging on the ends.
The harsh conditions and inhospitable winters, where the sun doesn't rise for months on end, meant IceCube took five long years to complete.
Thousands of sensors were spread over a cubic kilometer of ice, making it the largest neutrino telescope in the world.
And indeed, IceCube's bread and butter is high-energy neutrinos, produced by calamitous events in the deep, far-off universe.
And yet, it also has its subterranean eyes set a little closer to home.
For IceCube is on the lookout for neutrinos being hurled up from the core of the Earth.
Neutrinos produced by dark matter.
If dark energy had been an agonizing thorn in string theory's side, dark matter might yet prove a powerful ally.
As we've seen already, dark energy is the mysterious entity that appears to be accelerating the universe's expansion.
Dark matter, however, in a sense plays the opposite role.
It is the invisible glue that binds cosmic structures together.
Astronomers first noticed dark matter's effects as far back as the 1930s.
Galaxies within clusters seem to be moving too fast, and one way to explain why these clusters didn't simply fly apart is if there was hidden material inside exerting an extra gravitational pull.
Indeed, individual galaxies told a similar story.
Stars on their edges orbited faster than expected.
Perhaps, astronomers mused, they too were held in place by some invisible adhesive.
At first, though, scientists were stumped as to what dark matter could be made of.
The culprit seemed to have two properties.
It must have mass, otherwise it wouldn't exert gravity, and it must not interact with the light, otherwise we'd see it.
Unfortunately, no suspect in the standard model lineup matched that particular fit.
And so, they wondered, could dark matter be lurking beyond the standard model.
Astronomers interest in dark matter accelerated in the 1970s, just as string theorists were beginning to juggle with supersymmetry.
And it turned out that the lightest supersymmetric particle, the neutralino, would behave just like dark matter.
It is a form of weakly interacting massive particle, or WIMP for short.
And from that moment to this, the search for WIMPs gathered pace.
And so it seemed that supersymmetry didn't just streamline string theory, it also seemed to predict one of the most fundamental aspects of our universe.
Finding WIMPs, therefore, would be a ringing endorsement of supersymmetry and bolster the case for string theory, to boot.
And indeed, despite all its promise with dark matter, supersymmetry also had an older alibi.
After all, it was supersymmetry that first let string theory smuggle gravity into quantum mechanics.
Without it, string theory's cleanest prediction, the graviton, vanishes.
And without the graviton, the whole defense begins to unravel at a precipitous pace.
And so string theorists pinned their hopes on the detectors hidden beneath the ice.
If the galaxy is indeed flooded with WIMPs, the solar system should be plunging through them as it orbits around the Milky Way.
Dark matter particles should continually sink into the core of the Earth, where they would collide with one another and produce neutrinos.
Neutrinos that IceCube has been looking for.
Simple enough, except for the fact it hasn't seen any.
Indeed, a study released in early 2025 trolled through a decade of IceCube data and found absolutely no signatures of dark matter coming from the center of the Earth.
Perhaps scientists thought another team would have more luck.
This time with an experiment not tucked away under the Antarctic ice, but hidden a mile underneath South Dakota in an abandoned gold mine.
Except once again, the search here with the LUX Zeppelin experiment also came up short.
But perhaps the heady maelstrom of the galactic center, where stars and dust are constantly swirling around a gargantuan supermassive black hole, offers more positivity for WIMPs.
Indeed, another experiment has been scouring this region for clues.
The Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, bolted to the side of the International Space Station, AMS-02 is a hulking $2 billion cosmic ray detector.
Since 2011, it's been measuring high-energy particles that might be produced by WIMP annihilations near the galactic center.
And initial results looked promising.
AMS-02 found more positrons than expected, raising hopes that dark matter might be the culprit.
But again, the signal proved ambiguous.
Pulsars, rapidly spinning neutron stars, could produce the same excess.
This means that more than a decade on, physicists are still debating what, if anything, AMS-02 has seen.
And so, the result is frustratingly familiar.
Hints, suggestions, and shadows, but never certainty.
The evidence for supersymmetry through dark matter searches remains agonizingly elusive.
But, there is another way.
The most direct tests of supersymmetry have taken place at the largest energies achievable on Earth, at the Large Hadron Collider.
Here, beneath the French-Swiss border, protons are smashed together at near light speeds in the hope that something entirely new might emerge.
If super symmetric particles exist, some should be within the Large Hadron Collider's reach.
The LHC first turned on to much fanfare towards the end of 2008, and within 4 years it made headlines around the world when physicists discovered the Higgs boson, the much lauded god particle.
The Higgs boson and the associated Higgs field is what gives other particles mass.
And yet the discovery of the Higgs threw up a confounding mystery.
It was a lot lighter than physicists had expected.
With mass and energy interchangeable, the energy of the Higgs field was surprisingly low.
And this meant that supersymmetry became a white knight riding in to save the day.
This is because if ordinary particles have sparticle partners, they would partly cancel each other out leading to a low energy Higgs field.
Add in the ability to explain dark matter and the unification of forces at high energies, and supersymmetry seemed to hold the upper hand.
And yet, that cancellation only works if sparticles are also relatively light.
The heavier they are, the harder it is to use them to square away the lowly mass of the Higgs.
And this was the problem.
The LHC is smashing particles together with such ferocity that it should be producing sparticles at the lighter end of what is possible.
And yet once again, like IceCube and LUX, the silence was deafening.
The jury heard the harsh as loudly as any testimony.
As the prosecution pressed home the advantage, the defense scrambled for explanations.
Maybe light sparticles do exist, but somehow the LHC is missing them.
It's unlikely, but possible.
More likely is that if sparticles do exist, they're too heavy for the LHC to produce at current energies.
But that then makes it nearly impossible for supersymmetry to explain the featherweight mass of the Higgs.
To the jury, it sounded less like confidence and more like backtracking.
For decades, supersymmetry had been the defense's star witness.
Beauty incarnate, the promise that string theory could finally make contact with reality.
Now, that witness looked evasive, its testimony collapsing under cross-examination.
And even that still wasn't the end.
The higher the mass of the sparticles becomes, the harder it is to use supersymmetry to explain the full triumvirate of dark matter, force unification, and Higgs mass.
Physicists are forced to fine-tune the theory with surgical precision, undermining much of supersymmetry's original far-reaching appeal.
And so yet again, when confronted with a deluge of experimental evidence to the contrary, the defense team seems to squirm and wriggle its way out of it.
In an essay aimed at his peers, physicist Mikhail Shifman has urged them to stop developing continued, baroque-like, aesthetically unappealing modifications to supersymmetry.
It's a sharp prosecution argument with familiar sting.
Supersymmetry remains beautiful, but is increasingly edging ever further away from testable ground.
Once more, the defense team was forced to pivot.
Their original alibi, that supersymmetry elegantly explained the Higgs mass, was quietly shelved.
Now, a a theory once operating on the fringes was called to the stand, an idea that came, at least in part, from Nima Arkani-Hamed.
Arkani-Hamed was born in Houston, Texas, 10 days before Apollo 16 touched down on the lunar surface in 1972.
His Iranian father, Jafar, worked on the program for NASA analyzing the moon's physical properties.
After the Shah of Iran was overthrown in 1979, the family returned to the country, but it didn't last long.
Ayatollah Khomeini quickly began closing universities, and Jafar was an outspoken critic.
He was soon blacklisted.
He'd be hanged if caught.
Faced with little alternative, Jafar gave up his $50,000 to people smugglers who were charged with ushering Jafar, Nima, and the rest of the family out of Iran on horseback.
Except, it didn't go to plan.
10-year-old Nima soon developed a fever and struggled to walk.
Jafar ran for help.
Nomads leapt to the family's aid, carrying the ailing Nima over the border on one of their horses.
However, Nima's mother still feared he would die.
And so desperate, she pointed up to the Milky Way overhead and promised her son a telescope if they made it out.
She would later go on to say that she thinks her promise saved his life.
And that boy in the mountains would grow up to become one of the most daring minds in modern physics, a theorist unafraid to question orthodoxy, even when it means sacrificing beauty.
Colleagues have called Arkani-Hamed a Messiah, and indeed, according to physicist Raman Sundrum, Nima's persuasiveness is hypnotic.
A lot of people follow where he leads.
In 2004, Arkani-Hamed, working alongside his former advisor Savas Dimopoulos, proposed a radical twist.
What if supersymmetry wasn't beautiful and elegant at all?
What if nature has carved it in two?
This was split supersymmetry, where the symmetry is still real, but its effects are lopsided.
The particles that help unify the forces and account for dark matter could still be light, but the particles that protect the Higgs from quantum instability might be unimaginably heavy.
So heavy that the cancellation trick no longer works.
In a sense, split supersymmetry was a plea bargain.
The defense dropped one charge, that supersymmetry could explain the Higgs mass, in favor of doubling down on dark matter and force unification.
Together, these still aligned with the deep structural architecture of string theory.
Supersymmetry, even in this fractured form, was still playing by the rules.
But, once again, there was yet another catch, and this was a costly one.
By lifting the mass of the super partners to extremely high energies, far beyond the reach of the LHC or any foreseeable collider, split supersymmetry pays for its survival with testability.
The heavier the sparticles become, the further into the fog of inaccessibility they recede.
For the prosecution, this was the same old story.
A theory that once promised to be falsifiable at LHC energy scales was now hiding its most distinctive particles on energy scales we may never probe.
Experimental accountability was once again being quietly reclassified as optional.
And yet, having said this, the theory is not entirely beyond reach.
Split supersymmetry still predicts relatively light gauge gauginos, the super partners of the force carrier bosons.
They could remain within the grasp of future accelerators or maybe even cosmological measurements.
Split supersymmetry also retains viable dark matter candidates and its predictions for force unification could, in principle, be cross-checked against future data on effects such as proton decay.
And so, while most sparticles may be lost to us, the theory's fingerprints haven't vanished entirely.
And so, to the jury, the question becomes one of burden of proof.
Does the theory's ability to evolve in light of new data count in its favor, or is this yet another case of shifting the goalposts, a defense based on beauty once more slipping into evasion?
The defense was out of conventional witnesses.
What remained was the last resort.
Another radical reimagining of the case itself.
Beauty would return to the stand one final time, but in a form neither jury nor prosecution could have anticipated.
Since we can never know anything for sure, it's simply not worth searching for certainty.
But it is well worth searching for truth.
Thunder cracks as the swirling sea toys with a shipwrecked sailor.
Exhausted, he closes his eyes for what seems like the final time.
Yet the storm clears and the ocean calms.
The gentle waves then deliver the sailor to the safety of a sandy beach.
As the sailor wakes, he takes in his new surroundings.
A forest of trees buckling under the weight of plentiful fruit, a pool of fresh water, a sturdy shelter long abandoned.
The castaway is astonished.
Of all the places he could have washed up, why here?
He sits on the warm sand marveling at his luck.
Yet some would say he wasn't really lucky at all.
Indeed the question of why here can only be asked on an island where survival was possible.
After all, the dead could not reflect on their fate.
Within physics, this logic is known as the anthropic principle.
And in the early 2000s, the defense would come to rely on it to justify their case.
And one man above all others took up this cause.
A man who had been part of the string theory trial since the very beginning.
One of the trio of people who came up with the idea in the first place.
The defense recalls Leonard Susskind to the stand.
Susskind may have started out as the Bronx plumber's son, but he would become string theory's street fighter.
Arguably its most combative advocate in the face of all the hand grenades thrown in by the prosecution.
And the anthropic principle would be his counterpunch.
The controversial principle comes in two forms.
The weak anthropic principle simply states that the universe must allow observers like us, otherwise we obviously wouldn't be here.
Take for example the fact that the earth is at just the right distance from the sun to have liquid water.
According to the weak anthropic principle, that's no coincidence.
Indeed were it not so, we wouldn't be here to notice it.
If the Earth had formed at a different distance from the Sun, no one would be here to ask the question.
Like the sailor, we marvel at having been washed ashore on a habitable island, but of course we could never have emerged on any of the countless barren rocks where survival is impossible.
Similarly, if dark energy were more potent and the universe had expanded faster, galaxies could never have formed and stars like the Sun wouldn't have ignited.
It's no surprise then that we observe an expansion rate compatible with life.
However, the strong anthropic principle goes further, arguing that the universe is fine-tuned for life.
In this case, the right conditions for observers to emerge aren't just allowed.
Nature is compelled to produce them.
The emergence of life not some serendipitous fluke, but inevitable.
So, when it came to string theory's failings, Susskind used the strong anthropic principle to flip the script.
To the prosecution, the vast landscape of 10 to the power of 500 possible universes had been a fatal flaw.
The theory that was supposed to explain everything in fact explaining nothing.
But to Susskind, the seemingly endless string theory landscape explained exactly why we are here.
Physicists had long noted that our existence is balanced on a beautiful, but precarious knife edge.
An orchestra of particles, each with precisely tuned masses and charges.
Gravity is the conductor keeping time with just the right amount of pull.
Dark energy is the counter-melody, introducing just the right level of push.
And so how, despite seemingly impossible odds, is the universe so perfectly fine-tuned for life?
Because, said Suskind, it isn't the only one.

If the string theory landscape represents an unfathomably large number of different universes, with the constants of physics varying in each, then in which of those myriad universes are we going to find ourselves?
It's as though the landscape were a sprawling archipelago.
Most of its islands are barren, storm-lashed rocks where no sailor could survive.
But there are a few rare oases, places with the cosmic equivalent of fresh water, fruit, and shelter.
And just as the curious castaway could only wash up on one of those hospitable shores, so too can we only find ourselves in one of the universes where life is possible.
By allying string theory with the strong anthropic principle, Suskind was turning the very feature the prosecution were calling an unmitigated disaster into a cornerstone of the defense.
And he laid out his case in a 2003 paper entitled The Anthropic Landscape of String Theory.
It was a move that enchanted some members of the jury while enraging the prosecution.
Indeed, the defense was now claiming that string theory was the very reason the trial itself could even be convened.
No string theory, no trial.
By this logic, given that we find ourselves in a courtroom, the jury has to find in string theory's favor almost by default.
Of course, the prosecution was quick to object to what they considered scandalous circular reasoning.
To argue that a theory must be true, otherwise we would not be here to argue about it, wasn't evidence.
It was yet more sleight of hand, beauty somehow masquerading as inevitability.
And so, to counter what they saw as an absurdity, the prosecution turned to a big hitter of their own.
A man who would repeatedly and publicly clash with Suskind over his use of the anthropic principle to justify string theory.
The court calls Lee Smolin to the stand.
Like Suskind, Smolin is a New Yorker.
His own path to physics top table was hardly conventional.
He dropped out of high school due to boredom before talking his way into college.
From the outset, Smolin was an outsider, willing to challenge the orthodox approach.
And by the early 2000s, that challenge took aim squarely at Suskind.
The two men clashed bitterly over string theory's growing reliance on the anthropic principle.
At first, it was private emails, then literary agent John Brockman intervened, staging a kind of intellectual knife fight on his website Edge.
Each man would write one final statement, unseen by the other until both were published.
Smolin did not hold back.
"The anthropic principle," he wrote, "was so vague that one can get any conclusion one wants.
It cannot help us to science." "A theory that could never be falsified," he argued, "had no place in the courtroom of physics.
It was little more than philosophical hearsay." To Smolin, invoking the sailor's good fortune was no explanation at all.
It was survival bias dressed up as science.
And Suskind was equally cutting.
"Let's not put the cart before the horse," he warned.
"Science is the horse that pulls the cart of philosophy.
What critics dismissed as unfalsifiable, he reframed as simply not yet testable.
Then, he twisted the knife.
"What people usually mean," he added, "is that they themselves lack the imagination to see how to test the idea." Next came the alibi.
"Quarks," Susskind reminded the jury, "were once derided as unobservable, too.
No one could isolate a single quark, so critics called the idea metaphysics.
And yet quarks went on to become the bedrock of modern particle physics.
Indeed, ironically, it was quarks that had killed Susskind's original hadronic string theory decades earlier.
Now, he summoned them back as corroborating evidence.
The clash between Susskind and Smolin was more than a personal battle.
It was the entire trial in miniature.
Is string theory a bold, but unfinished science?
Or an elaborate ruse hiding beneath a veil of beauty and inevitability?
And so, after decades of claims and counterclaims, the long-running trial had at last reached its final stage.
It is time for the closing arguments.
For the defense, the allure of string theory is simple.
It is the only framework that has ever naturally united gravity with quantum theory without breaking the mathematics.
Other contenders for a theory of everything exist, like Smolin's own loop quantum gravity, but none have been able to explain such a wide range of phenomena.
And it's not like there hasn't been progress along the way.
Supersymmetry, the Green-Schwarz mechanism, the various dualities, D-branes, the holographic principle.
These aren't just beautiful mathematical concoctions.
They've become important tools in other fields.

From condensed matter and quantum information to black holes and nuclear physics, string theorists freely admit that many of their predictions are beyond the reach of current experiments, but one day that could change.
The absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
Black holes, quarks, and even parity violation were once dismissed as absurd and fanciful.
Now all three are mainstays of modern physics.
And so is it really so hard to imagine that strings vibrating across multiple dimensions could one day join that list?
Science often demands patience.
Like the cathedrals of old, a good theory can take more than a human lifetime to build.
Those who lay the first stones know they will never see the spire completed, but that doesn't diminish the importance of their contributions.
And so in a sense, modern string theory in the guise of multi-dimensional M-theory is a blueprint and a scaffold, not a finished building.
At its core, string theory has always been about beauty, the enchanting compass that has so often pointed physicists towards undiscovered truths, like fingerprints nature has left at the scene.
The defense concludes with an air of defiance.
If string theory is guilty of anything, it is only of being ahead of its time.
But of course, the prosecution disagrees in the strongest possible terms.
String theorists, they argue, have been blinded by beauty.
For nearly 60 years, the theory has labored on without a single shred of experimental evidence to support it.
Searches for supersymmetry, for example, the most crucial aspect that saves string theory from falling apart into a slag heap of tachyons and no parity violation, continue to fail.
And yet every time experiment refutes one aspect of string theory, it's seemingly put back together with an even more elaborate sticking plaster.
For theory that's supposed to be elegant and beautiful, it has metastasized into a monstrous chimera.
Beauty has become only camouflage, concealing contradictions behind a veil of aesthetic appeal.
A multitude of extra dimensions, Calabi-Yau manifolds, wrapped up M-branes, all of them necessary to save string theory's blushes, not one of them ever glimpsed in the real world.
And AdS/CFT, which predicts a curvature of the universe that's the opposite of what we actually observe.
But the most egregious overstep, the prosecution insists, is the string theory landscape.
The use of the anthropic principle to invert the case in string theory's favor is the final abdication of science's duty to predict and have those predictions falsified through experiment.
It is no longer physics as poetry, but physics as religion.
A compass that points in 10 to the power of 500 different directions is no compass at all.
And so, the gavel falls one final time as the jury retires to consider its verdict.
After days of deliberation, they finally return to the courtroom.
The jury is hung, unable to reach a unanimous verdict.
Some are dazzled by string theory's elegance.
Others, however, think it claims too much and explains too little.
The former notes that beauty has been both savior and saboteur.
It rescued string theory when evidence failed, but also lured it into existential cul-de-sacs that make it hard to support.
The judge has little choice but to declare a mistrial.
It is clear that the case cannot be resolved with the evidence currently before the court, and so the file is left open pending the arrival of testimony only the universe can provide.

Apple just unveiled fast VLM, a vision language model that's 85 times faster, three times smaller, and powerful enough to run smoothly on a MacBook Pro.
This could be the breakthrough that finally makes AI truly see and understand the world in real time.
Let's start with why this matters in the first place.
VLMs are the class of models that let AI systems handle both text and images together.

So instead of just asking a model to write you an essay, you can show it a chart, a diagram, a scan document, even a screenshot, and it's supposed to understand and respond to you in a meaningful way.
But here's the catch.
If your input image is low resolution, the model misses details.
But if you crank up the resolution, you run into a different problem.
Suddenly, your vision encoder has to handle way more data.
It outputs way more tokens, and that slows everything down.
both on the vision side and on the language model side.
And when you're sitting there waiting for that first token to appear on screen, that lag is what we call TTFT or time to first token.
That number matters and Apple's been obsessed with it in this project.
Over the years, researchers have tried all sorts of tricks to make vision language models faster and smarter.
Some of the earliest systems like Frozen and Florence relied on a method called cross attention.
Basically weaving together the image and text inside the layers of the language model so they could interact more closely.
Later on the field shifted toward auto reggressive approaches, things like lava and plug owl, mini GPT4, Cambrian one, and plenty of others.
These models don't bother weaving image and text together in the middle.
Instead, they just feed the image information right alongside the text, letting the language model process both streams at once.
The go-to engine for handling images in most of these systems has been clip style transformers.
Variants like SIGLIP, AVA clip, intern VIT, and DFN clip are everywhere because they're reliable and well tested.
But they come with a catch.
They pump out a huge number of visual tokens which bogs down the rest of the system.
To fix that, people have experimented with pruning, cutting down the token count on the flaw.
Approaches like lava primemerge or matrioska token sampling were designed specifically for this.
At the same time, another group of researchers started moving away from flat transformer designs and toward what's called hierarchical backbones.
With setups like convex or fastfitit, the image gets progressively downsampled in stages so you end up with fewer denser tokens and avoid being overwhelmed by raw data.
And not too long ago, a model called conlava came out that ditched transformers altogether for the vision side, relying purely on convolutions.
Apple looked at all of this, the pruning tricks, the hybrid models, the full convolutional encoders, and decided to go one step further.
That's where Fast VM comes in built around a component they call Fast Vit HD.
At its core, Fast Vit HD is a hybrid vision encoder, meaning it mixes convolutional layers with transformer layers.
The convolutional part does the heavy lifting of compressing the image, pulling out local details quickly and efficiently.

The transformer part then takes over handling the bigger picture, making sure the relationships between different parts of the image are preserved and refined before passing the information on to the language model.
Brilliance of Fast Vit HD is that it produces far fewer tokens than traditional approaches.
Yet, it doesn't lose the fine details that matter for highresolution images.
And it's built to keep latency, the time you wait before the model starts generating words, as low as possible.
To understand why this matters, think about how most hybrid models like Fast Vit work.
They use four stages to gradually shrink the image.
Apple added a fifth stage with an extra downsampling layer.
So instead of the self attention mechanism operating on data reduced by a factor of 16, it now works on data reduced by 32.
That single adjustment means the encoder runs faster and ends up producing four times fewer tokens for the language model to process.
The architecture is carefully balanced up front.
There are three stages built around rep mixer blocks which are highly efficient for convolutional processing.
After that come two stages powered by multi-headed self attention which bring in the transformer's ability to reason over the entire image.
Together, this setup delivers both efficiency and accuracy.
Fewer tokens, less lag, and no major sacrifice in detail.
Numbers tell the story better than anything.
In the Lava 1.5 setup, fast VLM gets a 3.2 times improvement in TTFT against Lava 1 Vision at its maximum resolution of 1152 by 1152.
Fast VLM runs 85 times faster on TTFT with a vision encoder that's 3.4 times smaller.
And these aren't just speed tricks.
It's also matching or beating the benchmarks.
On text VQA, it's 8.4% better than Conva.
On doc VQA, 12.5% better.
And across a broad set of benchmarks like Seedbench, MMU, and MMVET, it's either matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models, often while generating five times fewer visual tokens.
When they compare it against Cambrian 1, which is a pretty strong multimodal model using multiple encoders, fast VLM is nearly eight times faster.
The training setup itself is surprisingly efficient, too.
Apple trained these models on a single node with eight Nvidia H180 GPUs.
Stage one of training that only takes around 30 minutes with a Quinn27B decoder.
Stage 1.5 where they do resolution scaling with 15 million samples is longer.
About 77 hours if you're training at 1024 resolution.
Stage two, the visual instruction tuning with 1.1 million samples takes about 8 hours.
And if you scale further with 12 1.5 million highquality instruction tuning samples, you get even more performance gains.
Apple also released multiple checkpoints, R4, R12, R41, and so on, so the community can dig in and test different training stages.
Now, one of the clever things about this work is how they approached scaling instead of doing fancy token pruning or tiling strategies.
They realized you could just scale the input resolution directly thanks to how fast Vid HD is designed.

So rather than chopping up your image into tiles like any res or sphinx and then processing each tile independently, fast VLM can just take the full highresolution image, encode it efficiently and still keep latency down.
They did test tiling though and found that at extreme resolutions like 1536 x 1536, tiling can still help, but in most cases direct scaling was better for both accuracy and latency.
The design of Fast Vid HD is surprisingly lightweight.
It has far fewer moving parts than the giant models out there.
Yet, it runs circles around them in speed.
On a regular MacBook Pro, it's nearly seven times faster than some of the most popular vision transformers while keeping accuracy just as high.
Even against models built specifically for this kind of task, like Vitamin, it's not only faster, but also smaller, which means it's more efficient all around.
Apple also tested how well speed and accuracy balance out, and the results are clear.
If you crank up resolution but pair it with a weak language model, the system wastes time.
But with the right balance, say medium resolution and a solid LLM, you get both speed and precision.
And compared to previous models, FastFit HD consistently gives better answers without the lag.
What makes this even more exciting is that Apple ran all these tests on actual consumer hardware, not some massive server farm.
They converted the model so it could run directly on the Mac neural engine and it performed brilliantly.
That shows this isn't just a research toy.
This is tech that could realistically run on your own devices in the future.
And while other teams tried complicated tricks to cut down on the number of tokens these systems generate, Apple's design just does it naturally.
At lower resolutions, it spits out as few as 16 tokens and still outperforms competitors that produce 10 times more.
In other words, they solved the problem at the root instead of patching it later.
The flexibility is another win.
Whether you pair it with smaller language models like Quinn 2.5B or bigger ones like Quinn 27B, it still shines.
Even with the tiny LLM, it beats older models by a huge margin, sometimes more than 80 times faster.
With the bigger LLM, it competes with the giants of the field while using just a fraction of the resources.
And in benchmarks that focus on tough textheavy tasks, things like OCR, document understanding, and chart analysis.
Fast VLM pulls ahead.

Fast VLM gets the same or better results with just over a hundred tokens.

Inception Labs just released Mercury 2, a diffusion language model pushing past 1,000 tokens per second while still handling real reasoning tasks.
And that combination forces a rethink of how modern LLMs are built.
For the past few years, almost every big language model you've used has been built on the same basic idea.
You ask a question, the model predicts the next token, then the next one, then the next one, and it keeps going until the answer is finished.
That approach worked well enough to get us chat bots, code assistance, and early agents into production.
Yet, it also locked the entire industry into a speed and cost ceiling that no amount of clever infrastructure could fully break.
This model steps around that ceiling instead of trying to punch through it.
It comes from Inception Labs, a PaloAlto startup founded by researchers who helped invent diffusion itself.
The same core idea that powers image and video generators like Midjourney and Sora.
Instead of treating language as something that must be generated one word after another, Mercury 2 treats the entire response as something that can be refined all at once.
The system starts with something closer to structured noise, then repeatedly cleans it up in parallel until the answer snaps into place.
That single shift changes everything about latency, cost, and how reasoning behaves at inference time.
Quick note for transparency.
Inception Labs gave us early access so we could make this breakdown.
They didn't review this video, and this analysis reflects our own take.
As always, when you see the numbers, they look exaggerated until you understand why they exist.
The model pushes just over 1,000 tokens per second in real world benchmarking.
Claude 4.5 Haiku sits around 89 tokens per second.
GPT5 mini lands in the low7s.
This isn't a small optimization gap.
This is a different speed class entirely and it comes from the architecture itself rather than special hardware tricks or aggressive shortcuts.
What makes this more interesting than a raw speed flex is that Mercury 2 is a reasoning model.
It solves multi-step problems.
It works with structured outputs.
And it runs agent loops without the usual latency penalty stacking up at every step.
That combination is the real story here.
Reasoning usually slows models down.
Every additional step compounds latency.
When you run agent workflows on traditional models, each call waits on the previous one, and suddenly even simple tasks feel sluggish in real products.
This AI changes that dynamic because reasoning happens inside a diffusion process that refineses the whole answer together.
The system can adjust, correct, and improve across many tokens at once, which keeps reasoning fast instead of dragging it out.
A good way to think about it is editing versus typing.
Traditional models type each word and move on.
Mercury 2 drafts the whole thing and keeps polishing until it's right.
That refinement loop gives it an edge and accuracy on reasoning benchmarks.
while staying fast enough to feel instant in production.
You can see that balance show up clearly in the benchmark results.
On AIM, which focuses on advanced mathematical reasoning, the model scores above 90.
On GPQA, which tests graduate level science reasoning, it lands in the mid70s.
Live Codebench, if Benbench, and instruction following tests all land in a range that matches or beats speed focused auto reggressive models while running several times faster.
These are not cherrypicked wins.
They're consistent across categories that matter for real applications.
Latency numbers tell the same story from another angle.
End toend response times hover around 1.7 seconds for this system in benchmarked setups, while comparable models take several seconds longer to complete the same tasks.
That difference is the gap between an assistant that feels woven into your workflow and one that still feels like a separate tool you wait on.
This matters a lot more than people realize, especially once you leave chat demos behind.
Voice systems need sub-second responses to feel natural.
Code assistants need rapid back and forth to keep developers in flow.
search, customer support, and internal tooling all depend on tight latency budgets where even small delays compound into friction.
Mercury 2 was clearly designed with those constraints in mind.
Another important detail here is how practical it is.
The model runs behind an open AI compatible API.
It supports tool calling, structured outputs, retrieval, augmented generation, and a 128,000 token context window.
That means you can drop it into existing systems without rewriting your stack.
You don't need to adopt a new paradigm at the integration layer to benefit from a new paradigm at the modeling layer.
Pricing also reflects that production first mindset.
Input tokens cost $0.25 per million.
Output tokens cost $0.75 per million.
When you combine that with the throughput gains, the effective cost per completed task drops sharply compared to slower auto reggressive models that burn time and compute one token at a time.
What's especially notable is that this model's speed comes from the architecture itself, not from squeezing performance out of hardware.
Most of the industry's progress over the last couple of years has focused on faster chips, better kernels, quantization, and distillation.
Those improvements are important, of course, yet they all work inside the same sequential generation framework.
Mercury 2 changes the framework.
The fusion allows multiple tokens to be improved per forward pass instead of committing to a single next token.
That shifts the entire speed quality trade-off curve.
It's closer to a step change than an incremental gain, and it lines up with what we've already seen happen in image and video generation once diffusion took over.
There's also a bigger scaling story hiding underneath this launch.
Auto reggressive scaling laws have delivered massive gains.
Yet, they're running into diminishing returns where larger models and more data yield smaller practical improvements.
Diffusion offers a different way forward.
One that focuses on how generation happens rather than just how big the model is.
The system proves that this approach works for language and reasoning at production scale, not only as a research demo.
Inception's background makes this less surprising in hindsight.

The founding team includes professors from Stanford, UCLA, and Cornell with deep roots in diffusion research and earlier breakthroughs like flash attention, decision transformers, and direct preference optimization.

The company launched in 2024 and quickly attracted backing from Menllo Ventures, Mayfield, Microsoft's Venture Fund, Nvidia's Venture Arm, Snowflake Ventures, Datab Bricks, and Innovation Endeavors along with individual investors like Andrew Ing, Andre Carpathy, and Eric Schmidt.
That mix of academic depth and production focus shows up clearly in Mercury 2's design.
What I find most compelling here is how this model reframes the conversation around reasoning.
For a long time, teams have treated reasoning as something you trade speed for.
You either accept slower responses to get better answers, or you keep things fast and limit how much thinking the model does.
It collapses that trade-off by letting reasoning happen inside a parallel refinement process.
The result feels closer to how humans actually work through problems, holding the full structure in mind and tightening it over successive passes.
This also explains why the model shines in agentic workflows.
When agents need to plan, act, observe, and repeat, latency compounds fast.

A system that completes each reasoning step quickly allows tighter feedback loops, better control, and more reliable behavior that turns agents from interesting demos into systems you can trust in production environments like IT operations, customer support, sales tooling, and internal automation.
You can already see the kinds of prompts Inception encourages creators to try.
Complex simulations, interactive visualizations, structured instruction following tasks, and constrain generation challenges all play to diffusion strengths.
These tasks benefit from models that can revise and align outputs across many tokens rather than committing early and hoping the rest works out.
Another subtle point worth highlighting is how it handles error correction.
Because the model revisits its output during generation, mistakes don't automatically cascade.
Early inaccuracies can be corrected in later refinement steps.
That property alone changes how reliable multi-step reasoning feels, especially on longer or more complex tasks.
All of this leads to a broader takeaway that feels bigger than a single model launch.
The industry has spent years trying to make sequential generation faster.
Mercury 2 shows what happens when you stop optimizing the bottleneck and remove it instead.
Diffusion already transformed image and video generation once it proved itself at scale.
Language looks like it's entering the same phase now.
If you're building realtime AI systems that need to feel responsive, integrated, and natural inside actual products, this AI deserves serious attention.
The real shift here is how inference starts to feel different at a fundamental level.
Faster responses open the door to product designs that simply weren't practical before.
Lower latency quietly resets what users expect from AI interactions, and strong reasoning running at speed lets agents do more work without breaking flow or testing patients.
Mercury 2 positions diffusion as a serious contender for the future of language modeling, especially in environments where speed and reliability matter more than headline parameter counts.
The fact that it already runs in production with Fortune 500 customers suggests this approach has moved well past the experimental phase.
So the real question is whether diffusion ends up reshaping how language models are built or whether this stays a specialized path for real-time reasoning.

The regional differences in opinions on edibility are from sources published before it was known that North American and Asian versions of A. hygrometricus were not always the same ; in some cases Asian specimens have been identified as new species , such as A. asiaticus and A. odoratus .
Although A. hygrometricus bears a superficial resemblance to member of the " true earthstars " Geastrum , it may be readily differentiated from most by the hygroscopic nature of its rays .
Hygroscopic earthstars include G. arenarium , G. corollinum , G. floriforme , G. recolligens , and G. kotlabae .
Unlike Geastrum , the young fruit bodies of A. hygrometricus do not have a columella ( sterile tissue in the gleba , at the base of the spore sac ) .
Geastrum tends to have its spore sac opening surrounded by a peristome or a disc , in contrast with the single lacerate slit of A. hygrometricus .

There are also several microscopic differences : in A. hygrometricus , the basidia are not arranged in parallel columns , the spores are larger , and the threads of the capillitia are branched and continuous with the hyphae of the peridium .

One species of Geastrum , G. mammosum , does have thick and brittle rays that are moderately hygroscopic , and could be confused with A. hygrometricus ; however , its spores are smaller than A. hygrometricus , typically about 4 µm in diameter .
A. asiaticus and A. odoratus are two similar species known from throughout Asia and Southeast Asia , respectively .
A. odoratus is distinguished from A. hygrometricus by a smooth outer mycelial layer with few adhering soil particles , 3 – 9 broad rays , and a fresh odor similar to moist soil .
The spore ornamentation of A. odoratus is also distinct from A. hygrometricus , with longer and narrower spines that often joined together .

A. asiaticus has an outer peridial surface covered with small granules , and a gleba that is purplish @-@ chestnut in color , compared to the smooth peridial surface and brownish gleba of A. hygrometricus .
The upper limit of the spore size of A. asiaticus is larger than that of its more common relative , ranging from 8 @.@ 75 – 15 @.@ 2 μm .

A. koreanus ( sometimes named as the variety A. hygrometricus var. koreanus ; see Taxonomy ) differs from the more common form in its smaller size , paler fruit body , and greater number of rays ; microscopically , it has smaller spores ( between 6 @.@ 8 and 9 μm in diameter ) , and the spines on the spores differ in length and morphology .
